https://www.politico.eu/article/israel-r.text: Israel rejected a U.S.-backed peace plan for Gaza Sunday, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu saying that Israel will not withdraw from the enclave until Hamas has been “genuinely disarmed.” In dismissing the 15-point plan drawn up by U.S. President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace , Netanyahu also said that as long as he is prime minister, “a Palestinian state will not be established” in Gaza or the West Bank. The peace plan announced by the White House at the end of July would require Hamas to disarm and relinquish its governance in Gaza, while Israel would be required to withdraw its military forces from the territory. Advertisement Advertisement Hamas has said that it would begin disarming, but in recent days an Israeli official said the country still had “serious security concerns.” The rejection is a blow to peace negotiations the Trump administratoin has been brokering since September. The U.S. president had described the plan, now rejected by Israel, as a “critical step towards Gaza finally being governed by a new Palestinian government” and giving Israel “the security it deserves.” Israel appears unlikely to pull back significant forces or make other concessions ahead of legislative elections scheduled for October. Netanyahu faces a tough reelection battle, with his far-right coalition partners urging him to keep up the pressure on Hamas and leave forces in Gaza. Opponents also accuse him of failing to prevent the Oct. 7, 2023, attack when Hamas-led militants attacked Israeli communities, killing about 1,200 people, mostly civilians, and taking 251 others hostage. Israel responded with a punishing military offensive that has killed more than 73,000 people, according to the Gaza Health Ministry. Netanyahu said on Sunday that he is now in discussions with U.S. officials about how to move forward. “They have ideas, some of which are acceptable to us and some of which are unacceptable to us, and we know how to stand up to these things,” he said.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: Serhii Beskrestnov with one of his working tools, a spectrum analyser, in front of a block of flats hit by a Russian strike in the Darnytsia district of Kyiv. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Serhii Beskrestnov with one of his working tools, a spectrum analyser, in front of a block of flats hit by a Russian strike in the Darnytsia district of Kyiv. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian Ukraine Interview ‘Nobody will win’: Zelenskyy adviser warns of mutual destruction if war with Russia continues Dan Sabbagh in Kyiv Serhii Beskrestnov says deadlock on frontline and increasing use of deep strikes is placing civilians and infrastructure at greater risk Sun 6 Sep 2026 00.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google R ussia and Ukraine are locked in an escalating war of long-range strikes with a growing risk to civilians in which neither side can entirely prevail, according to Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s defence technology adviser. Serhii Beskrestnov, widely known by his call sign, Flash, said he was worried about the prospects for Kyiv this winter, and suggested elderly people should be evacuated in case Russian bombing were to knock out the capital’s energy supply. However, the rapid wartime evolution also gave Ukraine the means to strike back, with plans to launch 1,000 drones a night to strike economic and military targets in Russia and halt its commercial air traffic, he said. “Now, this is a war of cities, a war of infrastructure,” Beskrestnov told the Guardian, describing a conflict that is essentially deadlocked on the frontline, with civilians at increasing risk hundreds of miles away. “In this war, nobody will win this game, because both countries, after the war, will have destroyed economics, infrastructures. So it’s stupid. We should stop this war. We proposed to Russia to stop this war, but Russia does not want to stop,” he said. View image in fullscreen The ruins of the Rozetka e-commerce distribution hub in Brovary, Kyiv, after Russian strikes in early August. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian Beskrestnov, 51, a radio specialist, was first appointed by the former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov as a technology adviser in January, before being taken on directly in July, after the latter’s dismissal. As Russian missiles rain down on Kyiv, casualties mount and the mood darkens Read more The adviser, who survived a drone attack on his home in April, agreed that “attack had become more powerful than defence”, because both sides’ air defences could not keep up with the number of missiles and drones available. Russia could engage in a sustained bombing of electricity, water and heating systems in Kyiv this winter with the high-speed ballistic missiles it was producing at a rate of more than 100 a month, Beskrestnov said. Earlier this week, Vladimir Putin said Russia’s military had been “ordered to prepare and carry out mass strikes” on Ukraine’s energy facilities, showing no sign of halting the war. “For me, it’s horrible,” Beskrestnov said. “We are talking about 2 to 3 million people, and Russia understands it can create a disaster in Kyiv.” City authorities should think about evacuating civilians in advance, particularly elderly people, he added, while emphasising he was not making an official statement. View image in fullscreen People gathered outside after a Russian attack in the Solomianskyi district of Kyiv last month. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian Ukraine is desperately short of US Patriot air defence interceptors, the main weapon capable of halting ballistic missiles, and Beskrestnov said he was “not sure” that Zelenskyy could obtain enough from abroad to prevent a crisis. Last month, the president said he wanted to secure 300 Patriot interceptors for the winter. Beskrestnov predicted Ukraine would “attack Russia more and more with deep strikes”, continuing a campaign that has resulted in factories, warehouses and oil refineries being bombed. “We have a target from our president to increase the quantity of attacks to 1,000 a day,” he said, rising from its current level of about 300. View image in fullscreen Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced this week that Ukraine would attempt to use drones to halt civilian aviation in Russia. Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian Addressing Zelenskyy’s announcement this week that there would be a sustained attempt by Ukraine to halt civil aviation inside Russia with the drones, Beskrestnov said: “I think it’s very simple: it’s not necessary for us to attack an airport, it’s just enough for us to fly at the airport and the airport will be closed.” Russia has also made a series of advances that have boosted its attack potential, including its first suspected use of artificial intelligence. Ukrainian investigators concluded that a simple Molniya drone that killed a person near a Zaporizhzhia gas station in July was being guided not by radio but by AI. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion “I’m just afraid what happens in the future because I think it’s just a question of time before Russia installs this technology in a Shahed,” he said, referring to the country’s standard long-range drone. It could render Ukraine’s “huge jamming network” obsolete without any radio communication to jam. Kyiv suffers hours of daytime air raids as Russia deploys new jet-powered drones Read more Beskrestnov said Ukraine was working on its own autonomous drones – “We have a prototype” – but that he believed Russia appeared to have more scale right now. Russia has also developed a new wave of drones and missiles powered by Chinese-made jet engines that can fly at more than 200mph (320km/h), faster than the first generation of cheap Shahed interceptors that Ukraine has developed. Moscow fired 2,500 jet-powered Shahed drones into Ukraine in August, up from 1,500 in July, and was planning to make “about 36,000 in 2027”, Beskrestnov said. It also planned to build another 30,000 of the slower piston-engine type next year. Jet-powered Shaheds are already being used to threaten Kyiv and other big cities for hours at a time, but they will be complemented by another 10,000 cheap Banderol cruise missiles during 2027, plus a further 10,000 Dan-T missiles, boosting Russia’s ability to bomb Ukraine’s infrastructure. View image in fullscreen People sleeping at Dorohozhychi subway station because of the threat of Russian night attacks. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian Four to six Ukrainian companies were working on jet interceptors, Beskrestnov said, but they were “not ready for final production”, giving Moscow a window of advantage. The adviser would not give a timeframe for when the interceptors would be ready. At present, fighter jets take the lead in shooting down jet drones. Civilian casualties have been rising as long-range attacks increase. According to the UN, 437 civilians were killed and 2,610 injured in Ukraine in July (the last month for which figures are available), the highest since March 2022. Accurate figures for Russia are not readily available. Beskrestnov said the dismissal of Fedorov as defence minister after a clash with Zelenskyy was “a pity”, though the change in his own role meant the scope of his work had expanded beyond the armed forces to include the national guard and across government. His role, he said, was technical and advisory and he sought to avoid becoming embroiled in personality clashes. “Don’t mix me with politics. Politics always has a part of garbage, rubbish,” he said. Nigeria said Tuesday it had recorded its first Ebola case of Africa’s latest outbreak, as Kenya declared its ninth case, prompting a regional health official to warn of ‘an extremely serious threat’. Photograph: Sebastien Kitsa Musayi/AP View image in fullscreen Children play outside a health centre in eastern Congo. Nigeria said Tuesday it had recorded its first Ebola case of Africa’s latest outbreak, as Kenya declared its ninth case, prompting a regional health official to warn of ‘an extremely serious threat’. Photograph: Sebastien Kitsa Musayi/AP Ebola Nigeria confirms Ebola case as outbreak spreads into western Africa Case in Africa’s most populous country was detected in a woman who had travelled from Uganda Associated Press Tue 20 Oct 2026 20.14 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Nigeria has confirmed an Ebola case in its capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus, the health ministry said. The woman began showing symptoms on 7 October and was admitted to a hospital in Abuja four days later, where she was later diagnosed with Ebola. It is unclear when she arrived in Nigeria, Africa’s most populous country. The health minister, Muhammad Pate, said authorities had begun tracing 44 people identified as contacts of the patient. “We are doing everything possible to contain this case by tracing all the contacts the individual may have had,” he said. Ebola cases in Kenya highlight US failures amid Trump cuts to key services Read more Uganda’s ministry of health said the patient had only transited through Uganda and that she is a Nigerian woman who had been on a business trip to Congo’s eastern region. The Nigerian authorities have not disclosed her nationality. “Travel through Uganda does not establish that infection occurred here. The location of exposure remains under investigation,” the ministry said in a statement. The ministry insisted Uganda has “no confirmed active Ebola cases”. Nigeria is the latest country to report an Ebola case as the outbreak spreads across the region. Kenya confirmed its first case earlier this month and has since recorded nine infections. Uganda had previously reported Ebola cases, but it later declared itself free of the virus. View image in fullscreen Health workers on the frontlines of the Ebola response receive vaccination in Beni, DRC. Photograph: Gradel Muyisa Mumbere/Reuters Dr Jean Kaseya, the director general of the Africa Centers for Disease Control, said on X that “we are facing an extremely serious threat,” with a fatality rate of nearly 50% of cases. “This Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak has already become the most geographically extensive in history, affecting several countries spread across three regions of Africa,” he said. The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control said two weeks ago it was stepping up surveillance following the detection of Ebola in Kenya and strengthening the country’s preparedness for a potential outbreak. “These efforts have focused on early detection, isolation and referral, laboratory diagnosis, infection prevention and control, contact tracing, risk communication and protection of health care workers,” the agency said. Nigeria established an Ebola taskforce in June after the outbreak in Congo in mid-May. The spread of Ebola beyond Congo has heightened fears among health authorities about the rapid transmission of the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has infected more than 9,500 people and killed more than 4,600 people. The latest Ebola outbreak is the fastest-spreading on record and is on track to exceed the deadliest on record, the 11,000 people killed in West Africa’s regional outbreak between 2014 and 2016, WHO has said.
